221: Hill completes the Seven Major Negative Emotions: the emotion of GREED, the emotion of SUPERSTITION, and the emotion of ANGER. He states that positive and negative emotions cannot occupy the mind at the same time—one or the other must dominate. It is your responsibility to ensure positive emotions constitute the dominating influence. The LAW OF HABIT will aid: form the habit of applying and using positive emotions, and eventually they will dominate so completely that negatives cannot enter. Only by following these instructions literally and continuously can one gain control over the subconscious. The presence of a single powerful negative thought or feeling in the conscious mind is sufficient to destroy all chances of constructive aid from the subconscious. Hill then discusses prayer: most people resort to prayer ONLY AFTER everything else has FAILED, or pray by a ritual of meaningless words. Because they pray only after everything else has failed, they approach prayer with minds filled with FEAR and DOUBT—the emotions the subconscious passes on to Infinite Intelligence, and the emotions Infinite Intelligence receives and ACTS UPON. If you pray for a thing but have fear that you may not receive it, your prayer will have been in vain. Prayer does sometimes result in realization—recall your actual state of mind while praying and you will know this theory is more than a theory.
222: Hill envisions a time when schools will teach the 'science of prayer.' When that time comes, no one will approach the Universal Mind (Infinite Intelligence) in a state of fear, because there will be no such emotion as fear. Ignorance, superstition, and false teaching will have disappeared, and human beings will have attained their true status as children of Infinite Intelligence. A few have already attained this blessing. If this seems farfetched, consider that less than a hundred years ago people believed lightning was evidence of God's wrath—now, through FAITH, we have harnessed lightning to turn the wheels of industry. People believed the space between planets was a great void—now we know it is very much alive, filled with mysterious substances and pulsating with energy, the highest form known except perhaps the energy of THOUGHT. There is evidence that this living, pulsating, vibratory energy connects every human brain with other human brains in mysterious ways. Why should we not believe this same energy connects every human brain with Infinite Intelligence? There are no tollgates between the finite mind and Infinite Intelligence. Communication costs nothing except Patience, Faith, Persistence, Understanding, and a SINCERE DESIRE to communicate. The approach can be made only by each individual—paid prayers are worthless. Infinite Intelligence does no business by proxy. You either go direct or you do not communicate.
223: Hill explains the method of communicating with Infinite Intelligence is analogous to radio transmission. Sound cannot be communicated through airwaves until it has been stepped up or changed into a rate of vibration the human ear cannot detect. Radio equipment takes the sound of the human voice and scrambles or modifies it by stepping up the vibration millions of times—only then can sound be communicated hundreds or thousands of miles. After transformation, the original vibrations—now highly energized electromagnetic waves—are broadcast to receivers, which step the energy back down to its original state as recognizable sound. Similarly, the subconscious mind is the intermediary which translates one's prayers into terms which Infinite Intelligence utilizes, presents the message, and receives back the answer in the form of a definite plan or idea for procuring the object of the prayer. Understanding this principle reveals why mere words read from a prayer book—while they may provide comfort and cause for reflection—cannot and will never serve as an agency of active communication between the human mind and Infinite Intelligence. Before prayer will 'reach' Infinite Intelligence, it is transformed from its original 'thought vibration' into terms of 'spiritual vibration.' FAITH is the only known agency which gives thoughts a spiritual nature. FAITH and FEAR make poor bedfellows—where one is found, the other cannot exist.
224: This page opens Chapter 12: THE BRAIN—A Broadcasting and Receiving Station for Thought (The Twelfth Step to Riches). Hill recounts that more than 20 years ago, working with Dr. Alexander Graham Bell and Dr. Elmer R. Gates, he observed that every human brain is both a 'broadcasting' and 'receiving' station for the impulses of thought. Under the right circumstances, in a fashion likened to radio broadcasting, every human brain is capable of 'picking up' thought impulses originating in the brains of others. He connects this to the Creative Imagination described in Chapter 5—the Creative Imagination is the receiving set of the brain, processing thoughts released by other brains. It is the agency of communication between one's own conscious or reasoning mind and the four sources from which one may receive thought stimuli: Infinite Intelligence, one's own subconscious mind, the 'highly energized' conscious mind of another person, and the subconscious storehouse of another person. Creative Imagination is the mechanism by which intuition and hunches spring out of thin air, and by which two or more people working closely together in intense concentration seem to anticipate each other's next thoughts, actions, insights, and even actual words.
225: Hill explains that when the mind is highly stimulated or stepped up, it becomes more receptive to thought impulses reaching it from sources outside itself. This stepping-up process is driven by powerful emotions, either positive or negative. Thought manifests as electrical energy within the human brain. Only highly intensified or 'energized' thought impulses are transmitted from one brain to another. Thought modified or stepped up by any of the major emotions is the only type that passes from one brain to another through the 'broadcasting machinery' of the brain. The emotion of sex stands at the head of the list for intensity and driving force. The brain stimulated by sex is much more highly energized than when that emotion is dormant. The result of sex transmutation is the increase of this energizing effect to such a pitch that the Creative Imagination becomes highly receptive to ideas, which it seems to literally pluck out of thin air. When the brain operates in this highly energized state, it not only attracts thoughts released by other brains but also gives to its own thoughts the feeling essential before those thoughts will be picked up and acted upon by one's own subconscious mind. The broadcasting principle is the factor through which one mixes feeling or emotion with thoughts and passes them to the subconscious. The subconscious is the sending station; the Creative Imagination is the receiving set. Along with these, consider the principle of autosuggestion, the medium by which one may put the broadcasting station into operation.
226: Hill reviews that through Chapter 3's autosuggestion instructions, one was shown the method by which DESIRE may be transmuted into its monetary equivalent. Operation of the mental broadcasting station is simple—three factors: the SUBCONSCIOUS MIND, CREATIVE IMAGINATION, and AUTOSUGGESTION. The stimuli for putting these forces into action have been described. The procedure begins with DESIRE. Under 'The Greatest Forces Are Intangible,' Hill states the world has been brought to the borderline of understanding intangible, unseen forces. Throughout history, people depended too much on physical senses and limited knowledge to physical things they could see, touch, weigh, and measure. We are now entering the most marvelous of all ages—an age which will teach us something of the intangible forces. Perhaps we shall learn that the 'other self' is more powerful than the physical self we see in a mirror. People speak lightly of intangibles, yet all of us are controlled by forces unseen and intangible. The whole human race has not the power to cope with nor control the intangible force wrapped up in ocean waves. We do not understand the intangible force of gravity, which keeps this earth suspended in mid-air. We are entirely subservient to the intangible force of electricity—we do not even fully understand what it is, where it comes from, or its ultimate purpose. Nor is this the end of our ignorance—we do not understand the intangible force (and intelligence) wrapped up in the soil and resources of the earth.
227: Hill continues that we understand little or nothing of the intangible force of thought—the greatest of all the intangibles. We know little concerning the physical brain and its vast network of intricate structures through which the power of thought is translated into material equivalent, but we are entering an age which shall yield enlightenment. Scientists have turned attention to studying the brain, and while still in the kindergarten stage, they have uncovered enough to know that the 'central switchboard' of the human brain, the number of lines connecting brain cells, equals the figure one followed by 15 million zeros. Dr. C. Judson Herrick of the University of Chicago stated: 'The figure is so stupendous that astronomical figures dealing with hundreds of millions of light years become insignificant by comparison.' There are from 10 billion to 14 billion nerve cells in the human cerebral cortex, arranged in definite, orderly patterns. It is inconceivable that such a network exists solely for carrying on physical functions incidental to growth and maintenance of the physical body. Is it not likely that the same system providing billions of brain cells the media for communication with one another also provides means of communication with other intangible forces? After this book was written, an editorial appeared in The New York Times showing that at least one great university and one intelligent investigator were carrying on organized research reaching conclusions that parallel many described in this and the following chapter. The editorial analyzed the work of Dr. Rhine and his associates at Duke University.
228: Hill reproduces a New York Times editorial titled 'What is Telepathy?' summarizing Dr. Rhine's experiments at Duke University. More than a hundred thousand tests determined the existence of 'telepathy' and 'clairvoyance.' Various percipients were asked to name cards in a special pack without looking at them. About a score of men and women could regularly name so many correctly that 'there was not one chance in many a million of their having done their feats by luck or accident.' These powers do not seem to be sensory—there is no known organ for them. The experiments worked just as well at distances of several hundred miles as in the same room, disposing of any physical theory of radiation (all known forms of radiant energy decline inversely as the square of distance, but telepathy and clairvoyance do not). They do vary through physical causes: they do not improve when the percipient is asleep or half-asleep, but when most wide-awake and alert. A narcotic will invariably lower a percipient's score, while a stimulant will always send it higher. The most reliable performer cannot make a good score unless he tries to do his best.
229: The editorial continues: Wright draws with some confidence the conclusion that telepathy and clairvoyance are one and the same gift—the faculty that 'sees' a card face down seems exactly the same as the one that 'reads' a thought in another mind. So far, the two gifts have been found in every person who enjoys either, always of equal vigor. Screens, walls, and distances have no effect. Wright advances the hunch that other extra-sensory experiences—prophetic dreams, premonitions of disaster—may also prove part of the same faculty. Hill adds that in view of Dr. Rhine's announcement, he feels privileged to state that his associates and he have discovered what they believe to be the ideal conditions under which the mind can be stimulated so the Sixth Sense can function practically. The conditions consist of a close working alliance between himself and two members of his staff. Through experimentation, they discovered how to stimulate their minds (applying the principle used with the 'Invisible Counselors' described in the next chapter) so that by 'blending' their three minds into one, they find solutions to a great variety of problems. The procedure is simple: they sit at a conference table, clearly state the nature of the problem, then begin discussing it. Each contributes whatever thoughts occur. The strange thing is that this method places each participant in communication with unknown sources of knowledge definitely outside his own experience.
230: Hill explains that if you understand the Master Mind principle from Chapter 9, you recognize this round-table procedure as a practical application of the Master Mind. This method of mind stimulation through harmonious discussion among three people illustrates the simplest and most practical use of the Master Mind. By adopting a similar plan, any student of this philosophy may come into possession of the famous Carnegie formula briefly described in the introduction.
